chapterTitle: Ch 36. Training for Robustness and Generality

concepts.title: Invariance in data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Data augmentation often assumes that target outputs are invariant to input transformations, meaning the label remains unchanged after the transformation is applied.
concepts.content: When applying data augmentation, we typically do not apply any transformation to the $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$ values. The underlying assumption is that the target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are invariant to the augmentations of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$. Specifically, if $y(\mathbf{x})$ is the true $\mathbf{y}$ for an input $\mathbf{x}$, we assume that $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta)) \quad \forall \theta$. For example, in scene classification, we apply augmentations like mirroring because mirroring a scene does not change its class label. However, in optical character recognition, mirror augmentation is inappropriate because the mirror image of the character 'b' looks like 'd'. Character recognition is not mirror invariant, meaning $y(\texttt{mirror}(\mathbf{x})) \neq y(\mathbf{x})$. This lack of invariance also occurs in molecular data with chiral structures, where a molecule behaves differently than its mirror image.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept exists to define the conditions under which simple data augmentation is valid. By identifying transformations that do not change the ground-truth label, we can safely expand the training set to improve model robustness without introducing incorrect labels.
concepts.recap_md: - Assumes target outputs are invariant to input transformations: $y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$.

key_passage.text: The assumption we are making is that the target outputs $\mathbf{y}$ are **invariant** to the augmentations of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$. Let $y(\mathbf{x})$ be the true $\mathbf{y}$ for an input $\mathbf{x}$; then we are assuming that, $$y(\mathbf{x}) = y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta)) \quad \forall \theta$$

motivation.text: For example, if our task is scene classification then we would want to only apply augmentations that do not affect the class label of the scene. We could use mirror augmentation, since the mirroring a scene does not change its class.

concepts.title: Equivariance in data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Equivariance in data augmentation involves transforming both inputs and target outputs simultaneously so that the relationship between them is preserved.
concepts.content: To handle cases where $y(\mathbf{x}) \neq y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, we use a more advanced form of data augmentation where we transform the $\mathbf{y}$ values at the same time as the $\mathbf{x}$ values using transforms $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$. This results in an augmented dataset of the form $\{T_{\mathcal{X}}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)}), T_{\mathcal{Y}}(\mathbf{y}^{(i)};\theta^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^M$. This requires that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an equivariance between the two domains, defined as $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}})) \quad \forall \theta$. This is standard when $\mathbf{y}$ has spatial or temporal structure aligned with $\mathbf{x}$, such as semantic segmentation. For instance, if we apply a random crop to an image $\mathbf{x}$, we must apply the same crop to the label map $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Simple invariance is insufficient for tasks like segmentation or object detection where the label is spatially dependent on the input. Equivariance ensures that when the input is moved or altered, the label is updated accordingly to maintain correctness.
concepts.recap_md: - Transforms both inputs and outputs to maintain the relationship $T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x)) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x))$.

key_passage.text: For this to make sense, we require that $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$ express an **equivariance** between the two domains, which means, $$\begin{aligned} T_{\mathcal{Y}}(y(x),\theta_{\mathcal{Y}}) = y(T_{\mathcal{X}}(x,\theta_{\mathcal{X}})) \quad \forall \theta \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{$y$ equivariant with respect to $T_\mathcal{X}, T_\mathcal{Y}$} \end{aligned}$$

motivation.text: To handle the case where $y(\mathbf{x}) \neq y(T(\mathbf{x},\theta))$, we may use a more advanced kind of data augmentation, where we transform the $\mathbf{y}$ values at the same time as we transform the $\mathbf{x}$ values, using transforms $T_{\mathcal{X}}$ and $T_{\mathcal{Y}}$.

concepts.title: Out-of-distribution
concepts.one_liner: Test data is out-of-distribution when it differs significantly from the training data in characteristics like resolution, category, or feature space.
concepts.content: Data augmentation works by broadening the distribution of training data, which can reduce the gap between training and test data. When test images look quite different from training data—for example, having lower resolution or containing different object categories—we say the test data are out-of-distribution relative to the training data. This effect is illustrated in (Figure 1.1.6), where training data from Caltech256 is compared to test data from CIFAR100. By adding variation through augmentation (like mirroring, cropping, or color jitter), the training distribution broadens so that the test data become more in-distribution relative to the training set.
concepts.motivation_md: Models often fail when they encounter data that looks different from what they saw during training. Understanding out-of-distribution data helps researchers use augmentation to bridge the gap and improve real-world generalization.
concepts.recap_md: - Refers to test data that differs significantly from the training distribution.

key_passage.text: We say that the test data are **out-of-distribution** relative to the training data.

motivation.text: Data augmentation adds variation to the training data, which broadens the training distribution. The result is that the test data become more in-distribution, compared to the training data.

concepts.title: Learned data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Learned data augmentation uses algorithms to automatically discover complex transformations, such as pose variations, that are difficult to implement manually.
concepts.content: While simple transformations like mirror flipping or cropping are easy to implement, they represent only a few of the possible transformations a model might need to be invariant to. For complex tasks like pedestrian detection, we may want the model to be invariant to pose variation. Because such variations are difficult to code by hand, we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the desired invariances or equivariances automatically.
concepts.motivation_md: Manual augmentation is limited to simple geometric or color shifts. Learning the augmentations allows for more complex, domain-specific variations that better reflect the real-world challenges a model will face.
concepts.recap_md: - Uses algorithms to learn optimal data transformations instead of manual coding.

key_passage.text: Instead we can use learning algorithms to learn how to augment our data and achieve the invariances we would like.

motivation.text: But these are just a few of all possible transformations that we might want to be invariant to. Imagine if we are building a pedestrian detector. Then we would probably like it to be invariant to pose variation in the pedestrian.

concepts.title: Generative data augmentation
concepts.one_liner: Generative data augmentation uses models like GANs or VAEs to create new training examples by perturbing latent variables.
concepts.content: One method for learned augmentation is using generative models, such as GANs or VAEs. These models are suitable because their latent variables can control different factors of variation. Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}$, we can create an augmented copy as $\mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w})$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$. Using various settings for $\mathbf{w}$, such as Gaussian perturbations $\mathbf{w} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2)$, results in a set of output images that are slight variations of one another. (see figure: Generative data augmentation `genaug`)
concepts.motivation_md: Generative models can capture complex, high-level variations in data that simple rotations or crops cannot, allowing for the creation of diverse and realistic training samples.
concepts.recap_md: - Employs GANs or VAEs to generate augmented data via latent space manipulation.

key_passage.text: Given a datapoint $\mathbf{x}$, an encoder $f_{\phi}: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, and a generator $g_{\theta}: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}$, we can create an augmented copy of $\mathbf{x}$ as, $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x} = g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{w}) \quad\quad \triangleleft \quad\text{generative data augmentation via latent manipulation} \end{aligned}$$ where $\mathbf{w}$ is a small perturbation to the latent variable $\mathbf{z}$.

motivation.text: One way to do this is to use generative models. Latent variable generative models like generative adversarial networks (GANs) or variational autoencoders (VAEs) are especially suitable, because the latent variables can be used to control different factors of variation in the generated data.

concepts.title: Robust optimization
concepts.one_liner: Robust optimization is a general approach in optimization literature that includes techniques like adversarial training to improve model performance under competition or uncertainty.
concepts.content: Adversarial training is a specific application of a broader approach known in the optimization literature as robust optimization. This general framework is used for various purposes beyond standard classification, including training generative adversarial networks, training agents to explore in reinforcement learning, and training agents that compete against other agents.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard optimization may produce models that are fragile to small changes. Robust optimization provides a mathematical framework to ensure models remain effective even under worst-case perturbations or adversarial conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - A general optimization framework for training resilient models.

key_passage.text: This general approach is also known as robust optimization in the optimization literature.

motivation.text: Adversarial training has many other uses as well, beyond the scope of the current chapter- it is used for training generative adversarial networks, for training agents to explore in reinforcement learning, and for training agents that compete against other agents.

concepts.title: Multitask training
concepts.one_liner: Multitask training involves sharing data between different tasks by defining a broader metatask that encompasses them as special cases.
concepts.content: Because data for any single task is often finite, multitask training allows for sharing data between tasks. The approach involves broadening the task itself by defining a new metatask, $AB$, for which tasks $A$ and $B$ are special cases. For example, data imputation is a metatask that includes both colorization (predicting missing color channels) and inpainting (predicting masked-out pixels). A joint colorization-inpainting model can be trained on data from both specific tasks by treating them as general data imputation.
concepts.motivation_md: This technique addresses data scarcity. By training on multiple related tasks simultaneously, a model can learn more robust and generalizable features than it would from a single task alone.
concepts.recap_md: - Shares data across tasks by defining a generalized metatask.

key_passage.text: The idea is to define a new task, AB, for which tasks A and B are special cases. Then we can train AB on both the data for task A and for task B.

motivation.text: Because we have finite data for any given task, it can help to share data between tasks. In line with the theme of this chapter, one approach is to not just broaden the data but to also broaden the task.
